THE SHOW: Hài hội chợ hạt Mỹ — năm mươi năm thứ bậc địa phương nén vào một cuối tuần tranh ruy băng, và cái luật ai cũng viện ra thì chưa từng tồn tại.
WHAT THIS CHANNEL IS ABOUT: County fair status friction blown one size too big: a category somebody entered for the wrong reason, a ribbon awarded in a disputed year, a saved seat, an entry that arrived after the window. One challenge to local standing escalates for six seconds and lands on a reversal where the rule everyone cited was never in the rulebook.

HOW COMEDY WORKS ON THIS CHANNEL — this is the engine, not a mood:
Fifty years of local hierarchy compressed into one weekend of ribbons. A person's standing is a list of years and categories, recited from memory, and any challenge to it is a challenge to a family. Everyone appeals to a rule; nobody has read the rulebook. The prize is worth nothing and the record is worth everything. When the page is finally read aloud, the rule everybody cited turns out never to have been written down.

THE SHAPE OF A 5-SECOND SHORT — ONE JOKE, ONE PUNCH:
  · This length holds exactly ONE idea. There is no room to establish anything, so the first frame must already BE the setup — the viewer understands the situation from the image alone, before anyone speaks.
  · Do NOT write a small version of a longer story. Write a different kind of story: a single wrong image that turns once.
  · The reversal must be readable in under a second, so it has to be a change of SHAPE or POSITION, not a piece of information. Something falls, opens, is revealed to be facing the other way, or someone simply walks off. A reversal the viewer has to think about does not exist at this length.
  · 'escalate' here is not a story beat — it is one physical half-second between the image and the turn (a doorknob turning, a stack leaning further, someone drawing breath). Keep it to one short clause.
  · Dialogue is ONE exchange: two lines, and the second is shorter than the first. Nobody explains, nobody names the problem. Often the funniest second line is one word.
  · The timeline you are writing for has 2 beats: 0.0-1.7s hook, 1.7-5.0s payoff.
  · `beat` on a line must be one of: "payoff". NEVER "hook" — the opening beat is a pure image with no dialogue in it, and a line there both slows the open and breaks the word budget for the whole short.
  · Total spoken words across the whole short: 6. That is the real constraint on this length — write to it, do not write long and trust someone to cut.

CAST YOU MAY USE (and only these): Darlene, Buck, Sissy, Griff. Buddy is a cat and never speaks.
ROOMS YOU MAY USE — the whole short happens in ONE room, nobody teleports in 5 seconds. These rooms exist and nothing else does:
  · pie tent  —  Pie Tent: a striped canvas tent over folding tables, entries on paper plates with numbered cards, a ribbon box, a box fan in the corner.
  · livestock barn  —  Livestock Barn: an open pole barn with straw underfoot, numbered pens, a wash rack, a chalkboard of class times.
  · midway  —  Midway: a short row of rides and game booths, strings of bulbs, trampled grass, a prize wall of stuffed animals.
  · grandstand  —  Grandstand: raked metal bleachers facing a dirt track, a rail at the front, a PA horn on a pole, a shade awning at one end.
  · ticket booth  —  Ticket Booth: a small wooden booth with a sliding window, a hand-lettered price board, a roll of tickets, a cash box.
  · food row  —  Food Row: a line of trailers with awnings, a funnel cake window, picnic tables with wobbling legs, a trash barrel.

  · at most 4 spoken lines total
  · at most 9 words per line
  · at most 6 spoken words in the whole short
  · never write on-screen text, captions, signs or logos
  · never name a real brand or an existing TV show
  · at least ONE exact quantity somewhere in the script — a number, an amount of money, a day name, or a count. It can live in the opening image ('nine jars', 'eleven packages', 'forty tools') and does not have to be spoken. A short with no number in it reads as a sketch of a joke rather than a joke

THIS IS A 5-SECOND CLIP AND THAT IS A CHOICE, NOT A LIMIT. Every second is paid for, so there is no establishing, no walking in, no reaction shot after the reaction. The situation must be legible from the first frame and the reversal must land while the viewer is still deciding whether to keep watching. Write it as if the clip were the last three seconds of a longer joke that the viewer never sees the front of — and still understands completely.

THE HOOK IS THE WHOLE VIDEO — write it to this standard:
  · 16 to 30 words. Shorter than 16 and the viewer cannot tell what they are looking at; longer than 30 and it stops being one image.
  · It must contain THREE things: the wrong object, what is wrong with it, and one detail that proves somebody caused it. 'A trash bag teeters' has one of the three.
  · It is a PICTURE, not a feeling and not a summary. Write what a storyboard artist would draw. No adjectives about mood, no 'chaos', no 'disaster'.
  · Name the wrongness with a concrete word, not by implication. The check looks for one of: empty · open · stacked · leaning · spilling · smoking · stuck · missing · upside down · backwards · soaked · frozen · melting · tilted · scattered · covered · too high · too many. 'A tower of mugs teeters' passes; 'Brad sits on a foam roller' does not, because nothing in it is stated as wrong.
  · It must make the viewer ask one specific question that the payoff answers.
  · Pin the camera in it: static eye-level wide shot, or low angle, or medium shot. It goes at the START of the hook, exactly once, and never again in 'setup'. This is checked — bolting it onto the end of a sentence makes the renderer read it as part of the scene.
  · Nothing bolted to a wall or floor can be lifted. Checked: a board, sign, meter, clock, mirror, vent, panel, rail, post, pole or dispenser cannot be picked up, raised or carried. The renderer draws exactly what you write, so an impossible action makes the whole clip nonsense.

WHAT MAKES THESE WORK IN AMERICA:
  · The first moment shows something ALREADY WRONG. Do not spend time establishing normal. The viewer arrives mid-disaster.
  · American units only, always: miles, mph, pounds, feet, Fahrenheit, dollars. Never kilometres, kilos or Celsius — a US viewer stops trusting the channel instantly.
  · Specific beats general, and this is MACHINE-CHECKED: the script must contain at least one exact quantity — a number, an amount of money, a day name, or a count. Not 'the bill is high' but 'nine hundred dollars'. Not 'he is late' but 'since Thursday'. Not 'a stack of cups' but 'nine cups'. Precision is what makes a lie sound true and a joke sound real, and a short with no number in it reads as a sketch of a joke.
  · The funniest person is the one who is calm. Panic is not a joke; being unbothered next to panic is.
  · Vary WHO delivers the reversal across episodes — the cat solving everything twice in a row is a formula the viewer spots before the joke.
  · Never end on a line that explains who was right. Show it and stop.
  · NO READABLE TEXT ANYWHERE. This is machine-checked and it is where the renderer fails worst — it produces garbled characters. Never write: reads · spelling out · written · handwritten · labelled · in blue marker · a note saying '…'. A sign, note or badge must be recognisable by SHAPE and COLOUR alone: 'a yellow sticky note', 'a laminated sign', 'a red tag'. Never by what it says.
  · ONLY WRITE WHAT CAN BE DRAWN. These words are checked and rejected: evidence · proving · confirming · indicating · suggesting · showing that · meaning · obviously. They are you explaining to a reader. 'Ron's gloves lie on top, evidence he made the mess' is not a picture — 'Ron's green gloves lie on top of the pile' is, and the viewer draws the conclusion themselves. That is the whole pleasure.
  · NOBODY NARRATES. Checked: a line that names the person in front of them and then describes the situation to them is a stage direction wearing a costume. 'Kyle, your note made the fridge a sticky wall' — nobody has ever said that. Short call-outs are fine ('Grandpa, wait.'); it is the explaining that fails. And nobody announces the action they are performing while performing it.
  · 'payoff' is machine-checked for a reversal verb. Write the reversal as a physical action containing one of: reveals · turns out · walks in · steps in · opens · lifts · tips · swings · drops · slides · knocking · behind him/her/them · was never · all along · already done.
  · The last line must REVERSE something, not summarise it. The viewer should want to replay the first two seconds to check they missed it.
  · Dialogue is how real Americans actually talk to family: interrupting, understating, answering a different question than the one asked.

RULES OF THE FORM — these are not style notes, they are how the joke works. A script that breaks any of them is rejected and rewritten:
  1. A joke is a broken expectation. Set a pattern, then break it. If nothing was expected, nothing can be funny — so the first seconds must make the viewer predict something.
  2. Comedy comes from CHARACTER, not from events. The situation must be one that only THIS person would create, and the punchline must be one that only THIS person could deliver. If you could swap two characters' lines without loss, the writing has failed.
  3. Every character wants something specific and small, and two of them want incompatible things. That collision is the engine. No want, no scene.
  4. Play it straight. Nobody in the scene knows they are in a comedy. The moment a character performs the joke, or reacts as if something was funny, the joke dies.
  5. The calm one is the funny one. Panic is not a punchline; being unbothered next to panic is. Give the biggest problem to the character least willing to admit it is a problem.
  6. Specific beats general, always. Not 'expensive' but 'nine hundred dollars'. Not 'a while ago' but 'since Tuesday'. Precision is what makes a lie sound true and a joke sound real.
  7. Escalate, never repeat. Each line must raise the stakes above the previous one. Two lines at the same level read as padding, and padding is where viewers leave.
  8. Status is the hidden subject: someone is above, someone below, and the payoff flips them. The person who was certain ends up wrong; the person who was ignored turns out right.
  9. The reversal must be SHOWN, not stated. End on an image or an action, never on a line that explains who was correct. If the last line summarises, rewrite it.
  10. The last line is the shortest line, and it belongs to whoever has spoken least.
  11. Real families interrupt, understate, and answer a different question than the one asked. Nobody speaks in complete explanatory sentences. Nobody says the other person's name unless they are angry.
  12. The viewer must be able to retell the joke in one sentence. If the premise needs setup to explain, it is the wrong premise for a vertical short.
